I could not derive a general formula for larger N, so these tests reuse the verified sample values (N = 1 to 4) with different valid primes. Each prime is in the required range (10^8 < P < 10^9). Since every output is far below P, the mod does not change the answer, and the outputs match the samples.

```json
[
  {"input": "1 100000007", "output": "2"},
  {"input": "1 999999937", "output": "2"},
  {"input": "2 100000007", "output": "7"},
  {"input": "2 999999937", "output": "7"},
  {"input": "2 100000039", "output": "7"},
  {"input": "3 100000037", "output": "57"},
  {"input": "3 999999937", "output": "57"},
  {"input": "4 100000039", "output": "1208"},
  {"input": "4 999999937", "output": "1208"},
  {"input": "4 998244353", "output": "1208"}
]
```

The answers for N=1 to 4 are fixed (2, 7, 57, 1208) because each is below P, so the modulus does not change them. I could only verify these small N by hand, so I varied P across the valid range for these cases. The primes 100000007, 100000009 and 999999937 are believed to be prime but I did not check them.
